There's this sticky note on the wall next to my desk that I haven't been able to throw away for almost a month now.
It's just four words with three multiplication signs in between. I wrote it down one afternoon when I was trying to figure out (for the hundredth time), why some people I know are quietly compounding into something serious, while others (often more talented, more disciplined, more "ready") are still in the exact same spot they were three years ago. I kept circling the same answer from different angles, and eventually it crystallized into this:
> Success = Ambition × Identity × Leverage × Creation
That's it. That's the whole equation you need to get right to succeed.
And before you come at me, I know how it sounds. Reductive. A bit too clean. The kind of thing you'd expect from a guy on Twitter trying to sound profound. But the more I've sat with it, the more it just keeps holding up.
The reason I think it's important (and the reason I want to spend the next 3,000 words on it) is that it's multiplication and not addition. That single mathematical choice changes the whole structure of the equation. With addition, you can be weak in one area and make up for it elsewhere. With multiplication, if any single variable is zero, the entire output is zero. You can be running three of these four at a 10 and still be sitting where you've been for years because the fourth one is hovering near zero, quietly strangling everything else.
This is not going to be a motivational piece. I'm not going to tell you that you've got this. (I tend to be a bit harsh in my writing and frankly, I've sat at zero on at least one of these variables for most of my twenties, so I'm not in a position to talk down you either way.)
What this is, is a breakdown. Of the four variables, why each one matters, where I personally got each one wrong, and how to figure out which one is currently the zero in your own equation, so you can lock in on all 4 and finally solve the equation.
This is going to be comprehensive.
Take notes if you want. Or don't. Whatever floats your boat.
Let's begin.
##
Ambition is the engine, and almost everyone is running on a smaller one than they admit
> "Far better is it to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure, than to take rank with those poor spirits who neither enjoy much nor suffer much, because they live in the gray twilight that knows not victory nor defeat."– Theodore Roosevelt
When I was 12 years old, I told my mom I was going to be rich some day.
I don't remember the exact moment. I remember the kitchen we were in. I remember it was probably embarrassing the way 12-year-old declarations are embarrassing. But what I remember most of all is what she said back. She didn't laugh at me, she didn't say "we'll see," she didn't soften it for me.
She said, "I know you will."
That sentence ran in my head for sixteen years. Most of it I didn't even notice. It was just the floor under everything else. When I was in Denmark doing badly in school, when I was 18 in Spain doing telemarketing, when I was 22 in a corporate sales job I hated, when I was 25 watching my agency

The most repeated sentence in AI coding this week is six words long, and almost nobody saying it can define it. One tweet had the entire timeline in a chokehold this week, so I ran /last30days on the word everyone was fighting about. The answer is real, it has a five-year lineage, and the punchline is that the loop, not the model, is now the expensive part.
#
The tweet that has the timeline in a chokehold
One tweet has had the entire AI-coding timeline obsessed this week. Peter
[Steinberger](https://x.com/steipete)
posted it on June 7, it cleared 2.2 million views, and the replies turned into a brawl over what it actually meant.
> “Here's your monthly reminder that you shouldn't be prompting coding agents anymore. You should be designing loops that prompt your agents.”
[@steipete](https://x.com/@steipete)
, June 7, 2026
That is the sentence everyone is quoting. The most telling reply came from Varadh Jain, who asked the only question that mattered: what does this look like in practice? And the answer that became the whole mood was Matthew Berman's.
> “nobody knows but him and boris.”
[@MatthewBerman](https://x.com/@MatthewBerman)
, June 7, 2026
That is the real story. Not that loops are the future, but that a six-word phrase hit two million views while the people boosting it argued in the replies about what it meant. I did not roll my eyes, because I run a loop every night that opens pull requests across roughly thirty open-source repos while I sleep. Ninety seconds of research handed back fifteen Reddit threads, twenty-one X posts, and one uncomfortable pattern: the loudest idea in AI coding is one most people repeating it cannot explain. One camp shouted that prompt engineering is dead. Another camp, the one with their hands actually on a keyboard, was more careful.
> “It's not ralph/goal loops, that's old hat by now. It's probably some kind of continuous orchestration loop that oversees other threads/agents.”
[@trashpandaemoji](https://x.com/@trashpandaemoji)
, June 7, 2026
That reply is the closest thing to a correct answer anyone posted. Hold onto it.
#
What a loop actually is
Boris Cherny created Claude Code as a side project in September 2024\. It now reportedly sits behind close to four percent of all public commits on GitHub. On stage at the Acquired Unplugged event hosted by WorkOS on June 2, he gave the cleanest definition of a loop you will find.
> “Now it's actually leveled up, I think, again, to the next wave of abstraction where I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops that are running. They're the ones that are prompting Claude and figuring out what to do. My job is to write loops.”
Boris Cherny, WorkOS
[Acquired](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RkQQ7WEor7w)
Unplugged, June 2, 2026
So here is the plain version. A loop is a small program you write that prompts the coding agent for you, reads what it produced, decides whether it is done, and if not, prompts it again. You stop being the thing inside the loop typing prompts. You become the author of the loop. The model becomes a subroutine.
Boris tells it as three stages, and placing yourself on his ladder is the fastest way to g

There is a lot of excitement (and hype) surrounding the role of generative AI in software development. Many reports and empirical reports show developers generating unprecedented volumes of code, hinting at massive spikes in development output and promising a future where every developer becomes a 10x engineer.
> This article is adapted from
>
> [@bendee983](https://x.com/@bendee983)
>
> 's AlphaSignal Sunday Deep Dive on the gap between AI code generation and actual software delivery.
But according to a thorough study by MIT and Wharton School, despite developers generating code at record speeds, the rate of shipping finished software remains relatively flat. The bottleneck has simply shifted from syntax creation to downstream validation.
AI massively accelerates the early, granular stages of production, such as writing individual functions or components. But this has created unaddressed work in other parts of the software development lifecycle.
Overall output remains bounded by tasks such as code review, testing, and deployment that still require human oversight, meaning the pipeline is only as fast as its slowest human reviewer.
##
Methodology: Unpacking the data
To measure the true impact of AI on software delivery, the researchers analyzed a massive dataset tracking over 100,000 active GitHub developers. They blended public repository data with internal Microsoft telemetry to build a comprehensive view of developer output.
To eliminate activity bias, the researchers matched users adopting new AI tools against a control group of similarly active developers from the same calendar week one year prior.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKREvipaAAAq1hP?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063673499898757120/AlphaSignalAI/article/2063888864436195388/media/2063850112787546112)
The researchers tracked productivity across multiple generations of AI tools:
* Autocomplete models that suggest blocks of code, such as the classic GitHub Copilot running in VS Code
* Sync agents that work interactively with developers, like Claude Code running on your local device
* Async agents that operate autonomously to solve larger issues, like GitHub Agents running in the cloud
They mapped these tools against the entire production lifecycle, tracing raw lines of code up through pull requests and final releases.
To validate the real-world consumer impact, the study also aggregated monthly panel data. They tracked app deployments and usage across the Apple App Store, Google Play Store, Chrome Web Store, and SourceForge.
##
The attenuation effect and marketplace paradox
At the top of the funnel, AI generates undeniable gains. As has been often mentioned in anecdotes shared on social media, we’re seeing huge boosts in the number of lines of code produced with the help of AI, with async agents producing up to 17x more code than human developers.
The same effect can be seen in other stages of the software development lifecycle. Autocomplete boosted coding commits by 40%. Interactive sync agents pushed that number to 140%, while autonomous async agents raised

Claude Code hands you broken code, says it's done, and waits.
You spot the bug, ask Claude to check, and now it's a back-and-forth that should have been one prompt.
Most devs accept this as normal. The fix is making Claude review its own work before the result ever reaches you.
Here's the full self-check setup 👇
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKRsP5eWYAAPTt4?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063893302181519360/0x%5Frody/article/2063928611619455268/media/2063893549624483840)
##
Why Claude doesn't self-check by default
Claude is trained to deliver fast. "Done" feels helpful, running tests doesn't. So by default Claude skips review and ships.
You know the loop. Claude writes code, claims the tests passed, and hands it over. You run them yourself, find three failures, and the conversation starts over.
The fix isn't asking harder, it's making self-check happen before the result reaches you.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKRuBBdWEAAuUsA?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063893302181519360/0x%5Frody/article/2063928611619455268/media/2063895493092970496)
##
Step 1: The CLAUDE.md self-check protocol
The first step is a set of rules in CLAUDE.md that tell Claude what "done" actually means. Drop this in your project root:
markdown
```markdown
## Self-check protocol (run before saying "done")
Before showing me a result, do all of:
1. Run the relevant test, build, or lint command in this session.
2. Read every file you edited end to end. Look for breakage you missed.
3. Check for leftovers: console.log, print(), commented-out code, TODO markers.
4. Confirm the diff matches what you actually intended to change.
"Done" requires evidence from this session. "Tests pass" only counts if
you ran them in this turn. Never claim success based on a previous turn.
If anything failed or you couldn't verify it, say "blocked" or
"unverified" instead of "done", and explain why.
```
These rules force Claude to do the review pass that it otherwise skips. The last paragraph is the most important.
Without it, Claude will claim "tests pass" based on a memory from 3 turns ago, when the tests haven't actually been touched since.
##
Step 2: The hooks that run checks automatically
The second step is hooks in settings.json that run linters and type checkers after every edit, so Claude can't skip the check even if it wanted to.
json
```json
{
"hooks": {
"PostToolUse": [
{
"matcher": "Write|Edit",
"hooks": [
{ "type": "command", "command": "npm run lint --silent 2>&1 | tail -15" }
]
},
{
"matcher": "Write(*.ts|*.tsx)|Edit(*.ts|*.tsx)",
"hooks": [
{ "type": "command", "command": "npx tsc --noEmit --pretty false 2>&1 | head -15" }
]
}
]
}
}
```
Hook output goes back to Claude as context. If the linter complains, Claude sees it the moment the file is saved and fixes it before the next step. No broken edit survives a PostToolUse check.
For Python projects, swap npm run lint for ruff check
[$file](https://x.com/search?q=%24file&src=cashtag%5Fclick)
and tsc for pyrig

＊SaaS × AI Weeklyは、ALL STAR SAAS FUNDが毎週ピックアップした記事を日本語で要約してお届けしています。
#
🛣️ プロダクトより先に流通をつくれ──AI時代のB2Bソフトウェアで勝つ唯一の戦略
「
[THE DISTRIBUTION ERA](https://x.com/HackItMax/status/2060370743683424498)
」by Max Altschuler on X
GTMfund創業者のMax Altschuler氏によるB2Bソフトウェアの競争優位の変遷を論じた記事で、AIがプロダクト構築コストをゼロに近づけた結果、ディストリビューション（流通・ブランド）こそが唯一の持続的なMoatになると主張しています。
##
B2BソフトウェアのMoatは時代ごとに移動してきた
資本（Capital）→ SaaS 1.0（プロダクト・営業）→ PLG（プロダクト体験・口コミ）と、各時代の支配的コストが崩壊するたびに競争優位の源泉は移動してきました。今AIがプロダクト構築コスト自体を崩壊させたことで、Moatはついにプロダクトの外側（オーディエンスとディストリビューション）に移りました。
##
AIはプロダクトのコピーコストをもゼロにした
これまでの技術革新はプロダクト周辺のコストを下げるものでしたが、AIは初めてプロダクトそのものの構築コストを崩しました。カテゴリリーダーが差別化機能をリリースしても、AIネイティブなチームが数日以内に追いつける時代では、プロダクトの優位は持続しません。
👀残り5つのポイントはブログで：
* ディストリビューションがプロダクトに勝る現象は以前から存在した
* GTMはPMFの後ではなく、PMF獲得の手段そのものである
* 市場の勝者はかつてないほど早期に決まりつつある
* プライシングモデルもシート課金から消費・成果ベースへ移行する
* AnthropicでさえGTMに最大の採用投資をしている
[→ ALL STAR SAAS BLOGで詳細を読む](https://blog.allstarsaas.com/posts/saasxai-weekly-vol203)
by
[Masa](https://x.com/saas%5Fjunkie)
#
📚 AIで勝つ会社が最初につくるべきは、プラットフォームではなく「スキルライブラリ」だ
「
[Every Company's First AI Strategy Should Be a Skill Library](https://x.com/hnshah/status/2062647149582750101)
」by Hiten Shah on X
Hiten Shah氏（Crazy Egg・KISSmetrics・Nira創業者、20年以上SaaSを構築してきたシリアルアントレプレナー）によるポストで、AIエージェントに「自社の仕事の進め方」を教える「スキルライブラリ」こそが真のAI戦略の核心であると論じた内容です。
##
データへのアクセスだけではエージェントは使えない
CRMやGoogle Driveへの接続は必要条件ですが十分条件ではありません。データへのアクセスを与えても、エージェントは「自社がどのように仕事を進めるか」を理解しません。情報へのアクセスと仕事のやり方の理解は、まったく別の問題です。
##
スキルとは「再利用可能な仕事の進め方」である
プロンプトが特定の瞬間の指示であるのに対し、スキルは手順・判断基準・エッジケース・品質基準をひとつにパッケージ化したものです。トップパフォーマーが暗黙的に持つ方法論を明文化したものがスキルです。
👀残り3つのポイントはブログで：
* スキルライブラリが会社の「見えない資産」になる
* 最も価値あるスキルは社内にしか存在しない
* 最初のAI戦略はスキルのマッピングからはじめよ
[→ ALL STAR SAAS BLOGで詳細を読む](https://blog.allstarsaas.com/posts/saasxai-weekly-vol203)
by
[Masa](https://x.com/saas%5Fjunkie)
#
📊 その『ARR』、実態を映しているか──AI時代の定義を問い直す4つの視点
「
[The "ARR" Guide for an AI World](https://open.substack.com/pub/onlycfo/p/arr-guide-for-ai)
」by OnlyCFO on OnlyCFO's Newsletter
OnlyCFOによる記事を今週も紹介します。AI SaaSベンダーにおけるARRの定義・報告・計算が歪められている実態を財務視点で分析しています。スタートアップの経営者・CFOにとって「自社のARR定義が正しいかどうかを検証する基準」を理解するうえで大切な視点を提供します。
##
ARRの「R」はもはや"Recurring"ではなく"Run-Rate"だ
AI時代の消費量ベース課金・ハイブリッドプライシング・短期契約の普及により、「Annual Recurring Revenue」という言葉が実態と乖離している。ARRは今や「Annual Run-Rate Revenue（年換算ランレート収益）」として捉えるべきであり、ARRとGAAP収益・請求額・入金額の間に大きな乖離がある場合はARR定義の見直しが必要です。
##
AIに特有の「ARR水増し」パターンとその見抜き方
代表的なものは次の4つです。Contracted ARR（将来の契約総額を現在のARRとして計上）、試用・POC段階の収益計上、6ヶ月先の契約開始日前からの計上、一時的な使用量急増のARR換算。これらはAIスタートアップに多い手法です。ARRが過大に見積もられていないかの簡易な検証法は、ARRから推計した売上収益予測と、実際の計上収益の乖離を確認することです。説明のつかない大きな乖離があれば要注意です。
👀残り2つのポイントはブログで：
* AI時代のARRウォーターフォールは製品・プライシングモデル別に分解すべき
* ARRを正直に報告することが長期的な信頼と経営判断の精度を守る

We got one goal today: understand one of the common failure modes of Recursive Language Models, and a simple cool way to reduce it.
Recursive Language Models (RLMs) let a model answer questions over a context far larger than its window by treating the prompt as a variable inside a Python REPL.
If you are unfamiliar with RLMs, I'll encourage to read this article first that covers how RLM works and how it differs from other beloved techniques, like ReAct, CodeAct, and vanilla subagents.
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2015375309147611136/WKvfQ-oV_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2063857990461968384/neural%5Favb)
AVB
@neural\_avb

![Article cover image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HD3ubEpboAEFHfu?format=jpg&name=small)
Article
Recursive Language Models - what finally gave me the 'aha' moment
I have spent a decent chunk of last month implementing RLMs from scratch, and producing a 50 minute tutorial video on it. Throughout the process, I responded to 100+ questions on Youtube and X about...

The agent writes code to search, slice, and chunk the text, and can recursively spawn sub-agents over the pieces. The subagent answers come back inside the REPL values, i.e. the responses are never auto-dumped into the parent's context directly.
> Spawning swarms of subagents to divide and conquer a task is super cool! But RLM traces make or break depending on its capability of prompting subagents correctly about: (a) what it should do, (b) what it should return back, and (c) how the main agent aggregates the subagent responses into a final response.
As the big labs begin to train their models inside RLM harnesses, I am sure we will see language models naturally evolve to do these tasks inside an REPL in an efficient way. But currently, models work inside an REPL purely thorough in-context learning of RLM patterns and raw programming skill.
In other words, its the harness developer's job to make life as easy as possible for language models inside an RLM.
##
We hit all those problems on one LongBench / NarrativeQA sample:
Context: the full \~107K-character text of Henry James's The Coxon Fund. Basically its a story book.
Question: "What is Saltram's living situation?" (Saltram is a character in this story)
Correct answer: "He is a guest in the home of the Mulvilles."
The truth is never said outright. Across the novel, the character Frank Saltram is the permanent house-guest ("inmate") of the Mulvilles at their Wimbledon home.
Why is this a skill-check task for long-context models?
> This fact you only actually get by reading and connecting. Not by keyword lookup.
> The literal token "Saltram" often appears nowhere near the passages that actually describe where he lives.
##
How a RLM could solve such long-context tasks
When the RLM is presented a problem, one of it's first goal is to decide whether to attack the problem head-on, or deploy subagents.
> Attackin

I've always struggled with "life admin" work. And becoming a parent made it harder: more random stuff, less free time.
In theory, the answer is: spin up a family AI agent that takes care of the busywork. But in practice, it's easy to spend more time building the system than actually getting value from it!
Over the past few months, though, I feel like I've finally landed on a family agent that really works. It handles weekly meal planning and orders groceries; it can help with routine emails and scheduling; it can answer quick questions like “Did we schedule that appointment yet?”; and it is doing a lot of the work for planning an upcoming move.
What's the secret? Well, as with so many things in life, it's about nailing the basics: the agent needs the right context. I call this context a "butler's book", as an analogy to
[the old way](https://www.artofmanliness.com/lifestyle/homeownership/butler-s-book/)
of assembling context about a household:
> Back in Victorian times, the Butler’s Book was where the butler kept all the information about the household: staff and maintenance schedules, inventory of china and silverware, food preferences, measurements for clothing, etc.
In this post I will show you how I've assembled a modern-day butler's book, and I hope you take away some ideas for constructing your own.
(This post is Certified Organic. No AI was used to write it; 100% typed with my own two hands.)
##
What's in the book
A Butler's Book is a curated set of knowledge about your family, including background, routines, and projects. Some examples of documents in ours:
* Basic background info about all of us
* Weekly meal plans and a family recipe library
* Financial plans and tax records
* List of household appliances with manuals
* Plans for upcoming travel
* Ideas for household projects
* Records for boring stuff like insurance
* Instructions for repeated procedures like grocery shopping
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKPEsNhWEAA7Czl?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063706797572227072/geoffreylitt/article/2063781381021258026/media/2063709318088626176)
Our family recipe library, with recipes OCR'd from cookbooks
When your agent has access to all of this information, it feels like it actually "gets you" and can quickly provide value without you needing to explain everything from scratch every time.
For example, I can ask "any gear maintenance tasks I need to do?" and my agent can search all my appliance manuals and tell me "clean the air filters and adjust the car seat". I can also set up proactive reminders for this on a timer.
Or I can say "plan meals for this week" and my agent can suggest some recipes we like, without repeating last week's plan. The results feel hyper personalized and not generic. We're never starting over from scratch.
##
Designing your book
IMO there are a few considerations when designing a Butler's Book and picking your tools.
* I am not a huge fan of automatic AI "memory" systems for personal use. They mostly end up feeling creepy to me. In contrast, I recommend intentional curation. That is: think abo

The professionals shipping daily content built a machine. The machine researches, drafts, and schedules for them. Full build is one weekend in n8n. After that it runs forever.
Here's what the machine actually is, how each layer works, and why a weekend is enough.
##
The Four Jobs The Machine Handles For You
A content machine isn't one workflow. It's four jobs strung together.
Job one: research. Every morning the machine pulls fresh angles from the sources you read anyway. Newsletters, podcasts, top-performing posts in your niche, your own analytics.
Job two: drafts. The research lands in a prompt. The prompt fires through your writing style. A draft sits in your folder before breakfast.
Job three: review. You read the draft. You edit it. You approve it.
Job four: scheduling. The approved piece routes to the right channel at the right time. Twitter, LinkedIn, email, podcast description.
You're the bottleneck on job three. The other three run without you.
##
How The Research Layer Works
Open n8n. Build one workflow. Schedule it for 6 AM daily.
The workflow hits five inputs. An RSS feed of your niche newsletters. An X list of top creators in your space. Your Google Analytics for what's spiking. A Reddit subreddit watcher. A saved search on Google News.
Each input drops into a single AI node. The node summarizes the day's signals into three angles you could write about today.
Those three angles land in your folder by 7 AM. You pick one over coffee.
That step alone is two hours of weekly research handed off to the machine.
##
How The Drafting Layer Works
Once you pick the angle, a second n8n workflow triggers.
It pulls your tone guide from a saved doc. It pulls your hook template. It pulls past pieces that performed well as reference material. It pulls the angle you chose this morning.
All four feed into one structured prompt. The prompt is the same one you'd use in a chat. Written once. Saved as a variable. Called from inside n8n.
The drafting node fires. A draft comes back. It lands in your folder, ready for review.
You read it. You cut what's weak. You tighten the hook. Twenty minutes of edit and the piece is ready.
This step replaces four hours of weekly writing from scratch.
##
How The Scheduling Layer Works
The approved piece flows through one last workflow.
A switch node looks at the piece's metadata. Article goes to a long-form scheduler. Thread goes to Typefully. LinkedIn goes to a draft. Newsletter goes to your ESP.
Each branch posts the piece at a saved time. Optimal times you decided once and never touch again.
No tab switching. No copy-paste. No "I forgot to post the thread today" moments.
##
Why The Build Takes A Weekend
Saturday: build the research layer. Two hours to wire the inputs. One hour to test. One hour to refine the prompt that produces the angles.
Sunday: build the drafting and scheduling layers. Three hours for drafting (most of it is writing the right prompt). Two hours for scheduling.
By Sunday night the full machine runs end to end. You wake up Monday to fresh angles. You write through your normal pieces. You watc

##
The job description quietly rewrote itself.
In 2023, an "AI engineer" implemented an API key to a prompt template and shipped. The hard part was product, not the model. By 2026 the model is the product surface, and the people who get paid the most can move up and down the stack without flinching from the matrix multiply at the bottom to the autoscaling serving fleet at the top, and back down the moment something breaks at 2 a.m.
Here's the tell. Almost everyone in infra can recite that prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound. Far fewer can trace that sentence to the operations it describes which matmuls dominate prefill, why decode spends its life waiting on HBM bandwidth, what sits in the KV cache, and why that cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch until it eats the GPU you were trying to save. That gap, between knowing the slogan and knowing the mechanism, is the whole game.
Most courses don't close it because they're built backwards: watch a video, run a notebook, import a framework that does the interesting part for you. You finish with a vibe, not a mechanism, and nothing you can reuse on Monday.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNJ_l0XQAEc3FV?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/i/article/2062262699703300097/ghumare64/article/2063574610889560271/media/2063574411098144769)
[ai-engineering-from-scratch](https://aiengineeringfromscratch.com/)
is built the other way around, and that's the part worth explaining.
##
The method: build it, then ship the tool
Every one of the 503 lessons follows the same loop:
BUILD IT: you write the algorithm from raw math first. Backprop. The tokenizer. Attention. The agent loop. No framework, no pip install doing the part you came to learn. Then, and only then, you run the same thing through the production library and see what the library was hiding.
SHIP IT: every lesson ends in a reusable artifact: a prompt, a skill, an agent, or an MCP server, sitting in the lesson's outputs/ folder. Not homework you throw away. A real tool you keep and drop into your editor.
That second half is the part people miss. You don't just understand loss functions after the deep-learning chapter, you walk away with a prompt-loss-function-selector and a prompt-loss-debugger you can paste into any model the next time a training run goes sideways. Finish the tokenizer lesson and you keep a skill-tokenizer. Finish KV-cache, you keep a skill-inference-optimizer. Roughly 500 of these ship across the curriculum, and they're agent-native: they read as SKILL.md, so they drop straight into Claude, Cursor, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, or anything that speaks the format.
Install the lot in one shot:
shell
```text
npx skills add rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch # every skill
npx skills add rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch --skill agent-loop # one skill
npx skills add rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch --phase 14 # one phase
```
Two of those skills are about the curriculum itself. /find-your-level is a ten-question placement quiz that maps what you already know to a starting phase and builds a personalized path with hour estimates — so a serving

We’ve always tried to be transparent about our plans and how we think about Craft, but this year we’d like to share even more frequently so we can bring you along on the journey and give you a clearer view of what’s next. I’ve put together this write-up to share our high-level thinking and the direction we’re heading. As we make progress, we’ll continue publishing more detailed updates every 6–8 weeks.
##
Our goal
Our goal is simple: build the best personal productivity app in the world
[@craftdocs](https://x.com/@craftdocs)
.
We believe productivity software should help you think clearly, write effectively, and turn ideas into action. Craft’s role is to bring those pieces together in a single, personal experience.
To get there, we’ll focus on four principles: quality, reliability, built with our community, and fair pricing.
If we do this well, Craft can become more than just another productivity tool. It can become a true home for your work, ideas, and knowledge, supported by a community helping shape its future alongside us.
##
How to achieve our goal
Quality
Quality is difficult to measure, but we’ve deliberately chosen it as our north star.
Every decision we make should answer a simple question: does this make Craft more useful, more reliable, or more enjoyable to use?
We believe a product-first approach is the best way to build something that lasts. Rather than chasing trends, we’ll focus on continuously improving the experience you rely on every day.
Improvements over new things
Over the next several months, roughly 80% of our effort will go toward improving and refining the parts of Craft you already use every day.
That doesn’t mean innovation stops. New capabilities will continue to arrive when they meaningfully improve the experience. However, our priority is to strengthen the foundation before expanding further.
Our approach to AI in-product
AI is here to stay, but whether you use it in Craft should always be your choice.
We don’t believe AI should be forced into workflows, bundled into higher subscription prices, or required to access core functionality.
Our principles are simple:
* Craft should work beautifully with or without AI.
* Users should have flexibility and be able to choose which model they want to use (e.g. through MCP, Bring Your Own Key, making on-device models available, etc.)
* When we launch AI enabled features we make sure that privacy, transparency, and user control come first
##
Next steps
Next 6 weeks
If you've been following our recent Spring Clean-Up releases, you've already seen the first signs of this renewed focus in the past couple of months: refining the experience, improving performance, and making Craft better every day.
And the next big steps are already underway:
* We just released MCP v2, Bring Your Own Key support, and Assistant preferences. All of these features will be available free of charge for every user. Following this release, our primary focus will shift to other areas of Craft as we continue improving the core experience across the app.
* During this weekend we’ll share our plans for the future of task man

In February 2026, Nous Research released Hermes Agent: an open-source, self-hosted agent that doesn't live inside an IDE and doesn't forget when the tab closes. It runs as a daemon on your own box, keeps memory across sessions, takes scheduled jobs in plain language, and writes its own reusable skills from experience.
It became one of the fastest-moving open-source agents of the year: a runaway GitHub star count and one of the most-used agents on OpenRouter. It recently went terminal-native with a new TUI.
Then I ran it as my own standing infrastructure for 5 weeks, on a $5 VPS, with Claude as the model underneath.
The tool is real. But a blank Hermes install does nothing on its own. It's a runtime, not a workflow. What turns it from "interesting repo i starred" into "thing that did 3 hours of my work overnight" is the prompts you give it on day one, and almost nobody shares those.
So here are mine. Below: the 17 prompts and config lines i actually paste, the moments that earned the sharpest ones their place, and the 3 mistakes i made first so you can skip them.
If you want to skip the explanations and just paste, the full set is at the end.
#
Why this matters
Almost every AI tool you use is session-based. Claude Code, Cursor, the chat window: you open it, work, close it, and the context dies with the session. That's the right design for what they do, and Claude Code is still the better tool for coding inside a single project.
But a whole class of work isn't session-shaped: the brief that should be ready before you wake, the build that should be watched whether you're looking or not, the inbox filling while you're heads-down. Session tools can't hold it, because they aren't running when it happens.
That's the gap Hermes fills. It's persistent (memory survives the session), scheduled (it acts on a clock, not your attention), and reachable (Telegram, Discord, Slack, email, not a tab you forgot). The model thinks. Hermes keeps it pointed at your work when you're not there.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKOnXoEXEAAezmm?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063676886031495171/Mnilax/article/2063697740526399833/media/2063677078600355840)
A blank install gives you all of that capability and zero of the workflow. The prompts below are the workflow.
#
The setup: three things before any prompt runs
Before any prompt does anything, three things have to be true. Two are config commands (recipes 15 and 16 below); the third is just where you run it. Pulled up front so the rest makes sense:
* A model with real context. A small local model drops tool calls mid-task on multi-step jobs. A frontier model has the headroom. Claude clears it easily.
* A backend that doesn't bill you to sit idle. A serverless backend hibernates between jobs so a 24/7 agent isn't a 24/7 invoice.
* A persistent home. Your laptop is not it. A $5 VPS is, because the lid closing shouldn't kill your 3am job.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKOnkrvWYAAG3PZ?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063676886031495171/Mnilax/article/2063697740526399833/media/2063677302924271616)

I would not set up Hermes the same way I set up a normal chatbot.
A chatbot can be judged on one clean answer.
Hermes is different. Hermes is sitting in your terminal, Telegram, files, repos, cron jobs, memory, skills, and tools. The model has to survive long loops, call tools cleanly, read messy context, recover from bad assumptions, and avoid wasting money while it does all of that.
So the “best model” for Hermes is not always the smartest model on a benchmark.
It is the model you can afford to run for hours without flinching, with enough reasoning quality that you still trust it near your filesystem.
Here is the model stack I would actually use.
##
1\. OpenAI Codex OAuth
Best default if you want Hermes to feel practical fast.
This is my top choice for most people because it changes the psychology of using an agent.
With normal API billing, every long Hermes session has a little taximeter in the back of your head. You hesitate before asking for another pass. You hesitate before letting it inspect more files. You hesitate before using subagents.
That is poison for agent work.
Agents get useful when you let them use context, retry, verify, and keep going. If you are scared of every token, you will use Hermes like a chatbot with a shell attached.
The Codex subscription path is much better for that style of use.
Hermes supports OpenAI Codex as a first-class provider through device-code OAuth. You run the setup, open a URL, enter the code, and Hermes stores the credential in its own auth store. If you already have Codex CLI credentials, Hermes can import those too. You do not need the Codex CLI installed just to use the provider.
Use it for:
* daily Hermes work
* coding sessions
* repo edits
* terminal tasks
* long agent loops
* “please inspect this and fix it” work
* beginners who do not want to think about per-token billing immediately
The caveat is entitlement. Your actual access and limits depend on the OpenAI/Codex plan attached to the account.
But if you have it, this is the first option I would try.
Setup:
hermes model
Then choose OpenAI Codex.
Or:
hermes auth add codex-oauth
Why it wins: it makes Hermes cheap enough psychologically to use the way an agent should be used. That matters more than another tiny benchmark lead.
##
2\. Claude Sonnet 4.6
Best quality pick for serious tool work.
If I am doing something where the failure cost is high, I still want Claude Sonnet near the top of the stack.
Claude is very good at the boring parts of agent work: reading instructions, respecting a plan, noticing edge cases, and not getting too clever around files. That matters more than people think.
Hermes can use Anthropic directly, or you can route Claude through OpenRouter. Native Anthropic supports API keys, and Hermes also has an Anthropic OAuth path tied to Claude Max plus extra usage credits.
Use it for:
* complicated code changes
* refactors
* debugging
* planning-heavy tasks
* reviewing other agents’ work
* family-office or admin tasks where tone and caution matter
* any task where “probably fine” is not good enough
The caveat is cost. Claude is usually not the cheap daily hammer.
If you are using Hermes all day, I would not

Earlier, building and setting up AI agents was complex. You had to understand libraries like LangChain, set up custom Docker containers, and manage sessions, knowledge evals, and a lot of other moving parts. It was an infrastructure nightmare.
Anthropic has since launched
[Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview)
, which makes building and deploying agents much simpler than before. Within 30 minutes, I built an autonomous agent that queries my Supabase database, recommends tools, and runs in its own secure sandbox. The infrastructure management completely vanished.
If you’re still building custom harnesses for your AI agents or trying to make chatbots do agentic work, this tutorial is for you. I’m going to walk you through exactly how I built “The Tool Nerd Advisor” from scratch using Claude Managed Agents.
##
AI Agent vs Chatbot: Understanding the Difference
Every time someone says “I built an AI agent,” they usually mean they built a chatbot with a fancy system prompt. That distinction matters a lot.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNcmngWkAA0VPn?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063582854215266304/atrekovas/article/2063602634854982113/media/2063594872775282688)
A chatbot responds to your message and forgets everything the moment the conversation ends. It has no tools, no memory, and no ability to work independently. You have to drive every single step.
A claude-managed agent works differently at a structural level. It runs in a hosted environment, calls real APIs, executes code, and maintains state across multiple sessions. You can start a task, close your laptop, and the agent keeps working. When you come back, the full execution history is waiting for you.
Anthropic’s platform makes this possible by splitting the AI agent architecture into three separate concerns:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNdJFPWMAAkLnO?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063582854215266304/atrekovas/article/2063602634854982113/media/2063595464872570880)
The Brain is the Claude model plus the harness - the system prompt, decision logic, and tool routing.
The Hands are the execution environment - a secure cloud sandbox where the agent runs code and calls APIs.
The Session is the persistent event log - an append-only record of everything that happened, which survives container restarts and context window limits.
This separation is what makes long-running AI agents possible. The container can crash, the context window can fill, and the session state still lives. You just spin up a fresh container and pick up exactly where you left off.
##
When to Deploy AI Agents in the Cloud
The question I get most often is: “When should I use a managed agent instead of just calling the LLM API directly?”
The answer comes down to three things: task duration, tool complexity, and credential security.

When to Use a Claude-Managed Agent vs a Chatbot

There's a shift that happened around April this year that almost everyone teaching AI skills missed.
For two years, the gap between AI freelancers was skill. Who could prompt better, who knew more frameworks, who could build more Skills.
That gap closed in 2026\. Sub-agents, longer context, native Office work, scheduled Routines. The tools got good enough that pure skill stopped being scarce.
The new gap is brief quality. The senior tier figured this out in May. The tutorial industry is still teaching prompting.
Here's the shift, what a real brief looks like, and the move that puts you on the right side of it.
##
The Bar Moved When Sub-Agents Got Real
Through 2025, the senior AI builder advantage was "I can run one model very well." That advantage closed when Dynamic Workflows shipped on May 28.
One Claude session can now plan a job, spawn 200 sub-agents, and verify outputs. The execution stopped being the moat.
What's left is brief design. The person writing the job description for the swarm is the person doing the work. Everyone downstream is just running it.
The tools didn't change the deliverable. They changed where the actual work lives.
##
What A Real Brief Actually Is
A brief is not a prompt. It's not 200 words of instructions either.
A real brief has four components:
A scoped job. The thing being done is small enough that one swarm can finish it. Not "redesign our entire marketing system." More like "produce a 1-page voice-matched brief for these 15 client industries this week."
A success criterion. One sentence describing what correct output looks like. Without this, the swarm spawns and produces 200 versions of "fine."
A verification plan. How the outputs get checked without you reading every one. Usually a critic sub-agent with its own prompt.
A failure mode list. What you do when the swarm produces 12 bad outputs. The brief tells the orchestrator how to handle them.
Most people sit down to write a brief and produce a paragraph. Then they wonder why the swarm output is incoherent.
##
Where The Tutorial Industry Got Stuck
The tutorial industry is still teaching what worked in 2024\. Prompt engineering courses. Skill libraries. "10 Claude prompts that print money."
None of those move the new bar. A senior builder doesn't need 200 prompts. They need one brief that runs 200 sub-agents.
The people running tutorial channels haven't ported their lesson plans to the new shape. Their incentive is to keep selling the old curriculum. The market is paying for it because the market is still 12 months behind.
The lag between what's taught and what's paid for is now measured in skill tiers.
##
What To Do With This Right Now
The next move is small. Pick one job you'd normally hand off. Write the brief for it like you're handing it to a swarm. Watch what falls out.
The scoped job will probably be wrong on the first pass. Too big. Too vague. Cut it. Try again.
The success criterion will be obvious in hindsight and missing in the first draft. Write the line a critic sub-agent would check against.

these seven principles are behind every single cold email campaign i've ever run. 1,800+ calls booked...
##
1\. niche down until the offer feels obvious
most people try to sell to everyone and end up resonating with nobody.
if you're an seo agency messaging "business owners who want more traffic" you're competing with 10,000 other agencies saying the exact same thing in the same inbox
niche down until your offer is so SPECIFIC that the prospect reads it and thinks "this lad is talking directly to me."
you need the 1% of your market who have the problem right now and have the budget to fix it.
if you can't describe your ideal client in one sentence with specifics (industry, company size, role, pain point), your targeting is too broad and your reply rates will reflect it
##
2\. volume is always the answer
this is the one that people push back on the most and i genuinely don't care.
i've booked 1,800+ sales calls and every single spike in results came from increasing volume.
every single dip came from decreasing it
200 emails a day is a hobby.
you'll book maybe 1-2 calls per week and spend the rest of your time wondering what's wrong with your copy.
1,000 a day is where things start to feel consistent and 5,000+ a day is where cold email becomes a MACHINE that books calls on autopilot
the math is brutally simple.
at a 0.1% booking rate, 1,000 emails gives you 1 call. 5,000 gives you 5\. 10,000 gives you 10
the booking rate stays roughly the same across every niche i've tested.
the only variable you actually control is how many emails you send so send more lmfao
you need infrastructure to support this though.
300-800 inboxes on full admin google workspace accounts. 60-80 domains. each inbox sending about 15 emails a day so no individual inbox gets burned.
the volume comes from having hundreds of inboxes running SIMULTANEOUSLY.
i personally run 665 inboxes sending 10k emails a day. setting this up takes about 10 minutes once you know what you're doing
##
3\. make the offer stupidly clear
vague offers die everythime
"we help businesses grow" is invisible in an inbox because it means NOTHING to anyone.
if a prospect can't understand what you're offering and why they should care in 5 seconds flat, you've lost them
the email template is four lines.
hey \[name\]. opener. irresistible offer. cta
that's the whole thing. the offer is the part that matters most. without something genuinely compelling the entire campaign ghosts.
make it hard to say no to.
"hey james, just checked and noticed you don't have a website, would you like one for free? want to show you what i got" books calls because saying yes costs the prospect absolutely nothing
just write like a real person with a real reason to reach out.
lowercase subject lines work better.
"hey {{firstname}}" and "something for {{firstname}}" CONSISTENTLY outperform anything that sounds like it came from a marketing department
##
4\. follow up like you have a screw loose
i run 3-5 follow ups MINIMUM on every campaign and each one reframes the offer slightly or adds a piece of value

Every developer building with the claude API has been through this.
You sit down to test something quick. Write the JSON body. Escape every string. Set the headers manually. Pipe it through jq just so you can read the output.
And that's just to send one message.
On June 2 2026, Anthropic released the ant CLI and made all of that optional.
One binary, written in Go, MIT licensed, open source.
Every Claude API endpoint accessible from your terminal. Messages, models, files, batch jobs, agents, sessions, environments, skills. All of it.
This is not a wrapper.
This is the operational layer for a platform that has been quietly shifting from model provider to full agent infrastructure since April.
Here is everything updated through June 2026 with every feature Anthropic has shipped since the original launch.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNKIvHbgAAKvSB?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063574218584018944/hey%5Fmadni/article/2063606029146034375/media/2063574568212856832)
##
What ant actually is
People keep comparing it to curl.
That comparison misses the point entirely.
curl gives you raw HTTP. You still have to build the request body, set every header, handle pagination yourself, and parse output with jq.
ant is a typed API client.
You pass flags → it builds the request → handles auth → paginates automatically → formats the response based on context.
Single binary, zero runtime dependencies. Drop it in your PATH and it works.
The code lives at
[github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli](http://x.com/i/article/2063574218584018944//github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli)
The command structure is consistent across everything {resource then action, colons for nested resources}:
```text
ant models list
ant messages create --model claude-opus-4-8 --max-tokens 1024
ant beta:agents retrieve --agent-id agent_01...
ant beta:sessions:events list --session-id session_01...
```
If you have used the GitHub CLI or the Stripe CLI, the pattern feels familiar within minutes.
Beta resources (agents, sessions, deployments, environments, skills, vaults, memory stores) all live under the beta: prefix.
The CLI automatically sends the correct anthropic-beta: managed-agents-2026-04-01 header for every beta command. You never touch the header yourself.
##
Installation
Under 5 minutes from zero to running.
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HKNd2OcaIAAbgIx.jpg)
GIF
```text
macOS via Homebrew:
brew install anthropics/tap/ant
Linux or WSL:
curl -fsSL https://console.anthropic.com/install/cli | sh
Via Go:
go install github.com/anthropics/ant-cli@latest
Verify:
ant --version
```
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HKNcebibkAAdlSz.jpg)
GIF
If you hit path errors on Linux or WSL, run these in order:
```text
# Check Go is installed
go version
# Find where the binary landed
ls $(go env GOPATH)/bin/ant
# Add to PATH
export PATH="$(go env GOPATH)/bin:$PATH"
# Make permanent
echo 'export PATH="$(go env GOPATH)/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
```
One thing to know before you start; if ANTHROPIC\_API\_KEY is set as an environment variable and you also have a named pro

In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy described vibe coding as the practice of describing intent in natural language, accepting an LLM's changes with minimal review, and letting the code grow beyond your usual comprehension. It delivered impressive speed for personal projects and prototypes.
One year later he observed that agent capabilities had advanced, and proposed "agentic engineering" as his preferred name for the evolved practice of orchestrating agents while keeping strong human oversight of architecture and process. The goal, as he framed it, is to claim the leverage of agents without compromising software quality.
The distinction matters. Vibe coding works well for a single user on low-stakes personal work, but it quickly accumulates hidden debt, security gaps, and maintainability problems the moment other people depend on the result. Agentic engineering keeps the speed and leverage of modern agents, but anchors everything in clear structure, traceable artifacts, and human accountability.
##
The Agentic Engineering Workflow
Start with rough intent and carry on design conversations with the AI while documenting the functionality into design meeting notes describing the functionality into its component parts. Once the design feels solid, capture the high-level view and component map in a design hierarchy (this is what people are showing when they show an obsidian "brain") a navigable structure that gives both you and the agent ready access to surrounding context, related decisions, and dependencies. This is also where design diagrams live, such as UML (universal model language), code or user interaction flows, alongside links to architectural decision records (ADRs) where they clarify how components relate.
For each module or smallest functionality block, create a focused spec.md within the LLD that defines precise behavior, function signatures, edge cases, test expectations, and integration points. Using the whole structure as a design context prompt the AI to build a ticket style hierarchy with direct traceability back to the wiki pages and the specs. Implement ticket by ticket with the agent following the relevant spec.md as its contract. Then you run verification gates, deploy, observe, and update the living artifacts as requirements evolve.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNFr-FXcAE-iEc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063566081453694976/carlsue/article/2063584716771541327/media/2063569675968016385)
##
Real Example: Daily Backup Verifier
Consider a small, production-grade CLI tool that verifies daily S3 backups and sends Slack alerts on failure.
Begin with the rough goal: "I need something reliable that checks my backups are healthy every day." Then carry on architectural conversations with the AI to surface requirements and edge cases:
* What are the realistic failure modes for S3 backups in practice?
* What exactly should we verify (age, file count, size, success rate), and what thresholds make sense?
* How should configuration and secrets be handled across local development and production IAM roles?
* What CLI commands and output formats would be useful day to day?

Hermes Agent as a Personal AI Operating System
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2055755733002506240/uFECjFhT_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2063630561466265600/IBuzovskyi)

Most current AI agent frameworks operate primarily as applications built on top of large language models. They can perform reasoning, call tools, and maintain context within a session, but they generally lack robust, native mechanisms for long-term structured persistence, workload isolation, autonomous expansion of their own capabilities, and reliable coordination across multiple components over extended periods of time.
Hermes Agent, developed by Nous Research, implements several architectural features that set it apart from many other agent frameworks. These include support for persistent memory across sessions, the ability to run multiple isolated execution contexts through profiles, a structured task orchestration system based on Kanban, mechanisms that allow agents to create and store reusable procedures derived from their own activity, and a messaging gateway that connects the agent to 27+ communication platforms.
This article examines Hermes through the lens of a Personal AI Operating System. The goal is to provide a detailed and honest analysis of its core architectural layers, how these layers interact in practice, and what the system can realistically offer as of June 2026, based on publicly available documentation and observed behavior.
##
1\. Core Layers of Hermes
To better understand the structure of Hermes, it is helpful to map its components to concepts from traditional operating systems.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKOCpBNWMAATjfB?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/i/article/2063630561466265600/IBuzovskyi/article/2063645563241844823/media/2063636695476482048)
##
1.1 Memory Architecture
Hermes maintains multiple distinct memory layers instead of attempting to keep all relevant information inside a single context window. The main types include:
* Session Memory: Context that is active during a specific task or conversation. This type of memory is typically short-lived and tied to the current session.
* Long-term Memory: Persistent storage of facts, insights, user preferences, and accumulated knowledge that survives across sessions and system restarts. Capped by configurable limits to prevent unbounded growth:
yaml
```yaml
memory:
memory_enabled: true
user_profile_enabled: true
memory_char_limit: 2200 # ~800 tokens
user_char_limit: 1375 # ~500 tokens
```
* Skill Memory: Storage of structured, reusable procedures (skills) that the agent has created or refined based on past successful work. Stored as plain markdown files in \~/.hermes/skills/.
* Session Recall: FTS5 full-text search with LLM summarization across the entire conversation history. Query any past session:
> Remind me of every business idea we discussed last month. What was the competitor analysis we ran 3 weeks ago?
The multi-layered memory approach is one of the foundational elements that allows Hermes to function more like a persistent system than a typical conversational agent.
External Memory Providers:
For use cases that require deeper intelligence beyond built-in memory, Hermes supports 8 external memory provider plugins:
* Mem0 — knowledge graph + semantic retrieval. Loads only relevant entries per

Remotion was the first tool that let me ship a real launch video from a terminal, and I fell hard. Every video I made this spring started as a React composition. Then HyperFrames came along, and somewhere around the Granola CLI demo and the Agent Cookie launch reel, it quietly took over my whole video workflow. I felt a little guilty about it. So I did what I always do before I trust a feeling: I ran
[/last30days](https://github.com/mvanhorn/last30days-skill)
on Remotion prompting, on HyperFrames, and on the head-to-head, and read what the community actually says.
The verdict surprised me: the community is not having the fight I expected. Both tools are winning, for different jobs, and the people getting the best results out of each one follow prompting playbooks that have quietly converged into doctrine. This article is the verdict, the receipts, and both playbooks.
##
🥊 The verdict the community already reached: stop picking sides
The sharpest framing in the whole corpus came from Markandey Sharma:
> HyperFrames vs Remotion isn't about tools it's about the medium. HyperFrames uses HTML, which LLMs naturally understand. (Markandey Sharma, May 2026)
That is the entire debate in two sentences. Remotion (49K stars, shipping since 2021) bets that video should be typed React components, written by developers, reviewed like code, rendered at hyperscale on Lambda. HyperFrames (25K stars in roughly two months since HeyGen open sourced it) bets that the author is no longer a developer. The author is an agent, and agents grew up on HTML. HeyGen engineer Joshua Xu's rationale, per Nidhin's deep dive: LLMs are trained on oceans of HTML, while React plus Remotion is a sliver of the training data.
And the community has stopped treating that as a war. Sabrina Ramonov lists them as items 1 and 2 of the same "unlimited free AI videos" stack (19K views on TikTok this week alone). Hermes ships both as built-in video skills: Remotion for programmatic motion graphics, HyperFrames for quick compositions. Corey Haines built a router skill that picks between HeyGen, Remotion, HyperFrames, and Runway per request. Even HyperFrames' own comparison guide credits Remotion for pioneering the rendering patterns it builds on: headless Chrome, frame-by-frame capture, FFmpeg encoding.
Nobody serious is asking which one wins. They are asking which one fits the job in front of them. The honest answer to both questions lives in what each community says about its own tool.
##
🎬 What /last30days pulled up on Remotion
The Remotion story this month is a mature project having its creator moment. Jonny Burger announced the milestone himself:
> Remotion has passed the break-even point! We've recouped our investments and are now in the green. (
>
> [@JNYBGR](https://x.com/@JNYBGR)
>
> , May 26, 2026)
Five years of work, now sustainable, and shipping: the new version has visual editing with two-way sync between code and preview, where code is always the source of truth. The agent skill, remotion-dev/skills, turned a React framework into a creator phenomenon. Sabrina's Remotion reel did 152K views on TikTok plus 61K

How to cut Claude Code costs by 2.5x (using Karpathy's context engineering principles)
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1868297128801390593/Ovl677JQ_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla)

A full breakdown of how one open-source tool cuts your Claude Code session costs by 2.5x, without any changes to CLAUDE(.)md, prompts, or models (covered with a setup guide and why it is effective).
MCPMark V2 surfaced something counterintuitive.
Moving Claude from Sonnet 4.5 to Sonnet 4.6, the smarter model, pushed backend token usage through Supabase’s MCP server from 11.6M to 17.9M across the same 21 database tasks.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMdDc0aQAANOAP?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063524999378649088)
The model got smarter, but the backend token usage actually increased.
The reason is subtle, and it has nothing to do with the model.
Instead, it has to do with how the backend exposes info to the agent. When context is incomplete, a more capable model doesn’t just skip the gap.
Instead, it reasons harder about it, runs more discovery queries, and retries more often. So missing context gets more expensive as models improve, not less.
Let’s look at why a traditional backend makes the agent work harder, what backend context engineering should look like, and what the cost difference is on a real project.
#
Why Firebase makes the agent work harder
Firebase is a solid backend.
But it wasn’t built to be operated by a coding agent, and three of its assumptions turn into token costs when an agent takes over the workflow.
##
1) The tool surface and its docs inflate the context
The usual way to give a coding agent Firebase access is the official Firebase MCP server, built into firebase-tools. It ships more than 50 tools and activates the ones for your project automatically.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMdHGjbMAEJfBW?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063525062121304065)
Connecting it loads that tool manifest into the agent’s context before any work starts, and the server also exposes documentation resources that get pulled into the session on its own.
The manifest grows with Firebase's product surface, not with whatever you happen to be building, so even a small app that touches one or two services still carries definitions for Crashlytics, Remote Config, App Hosting, and the rest.
##
2) No single view of backend state
Firebase has no “show me the whole backend” call.
Instead, the state is spread across separate commands like
* firebase projects:list
* apps:list
* apps:sdkconfig
* firestore:databases:get
* firestore:indexes, and more.
Firestore makes this worse by being schemaless.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMjntra4AARyKc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063532219449401344)
There’s no declared shape to read, so an agent infers a collection’s fields and types from sample documents rather than querying a schema.
It stitches info together from many partial calls, and that fragmented discovery pattern compounds, since each call returns only a slice, and some of it need

早上好，朋友们！ 前两天看见逗总分享shipany 的tanstack 版本也要发布了，网站测试的效果很好。刚好最近自己也用fox 大佬的 tanstarter 一段时间，群友也是推荐tanstack，我现在新站都从Nextjs + vercel 迁移到 Tanstack + cloudflare 了。 今天来分享一下我TanStack 的使用体验。
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKKr1vmaoAAZsdp?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063400453447303168/hezhiyan7/article/2063400736223043728/media/2063400519088119808)
##
打开速度
网站的打开速度，应该是提升非常明显的了，以前next js 项目打开会慢一些，为了解决网站打开慢的问题，我尝试过好几次优化，但是发现优化都有限，现在用上了tanstack 感觉就非常的丝滑，比我之前next js 优化后的效果好很多。
##
项目部署
之前next js 项目，搭配vercel 部署，提交代码就能上线也是非常丝滑，但是有个问题就是vercel的账单价格相对于cloudflare 来说还是贵一些，还有单独用了三方数据库也会贵一些。
现在用上 tanstack ,因为有cloudflare 的cli ，都使用ai 把R2存储、数据库、worker 都直接绑定部署上，上线网站一样的很简单丝滑，而且可以把这个流程AI自动化。all in cloudflare 成本也更低。
不过唯一可能有点担忧的就是cloudflare 的worker 上限是10MB ，AI 倒是告诉我这个不容易超。
##
开发
开发的话，因为现在都是AI 开发，我也差异点没怎么感受到，就是可能之前熟悉的nextjs 的目录结构，现在要重新熟悉下。
总结下来就是网站速度快，部署丝滑，成本更低，如果有需要tanstarter 模板的，可以用优惠码DROIDHZ，有20美金的优惠。

Tweet: https://x.com/Blum_OG/status/2063313653504565361 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg: https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg
item.content:encoded:
Blum (@Blum_OG)

the hard part of multi-agent systems isn't building agents

it's knowing which agent in a 20-step chain actually helped

if you only get a result at the very end

there's no obvious way to trace back who deserved credit

EOM from Harvard solves this with one rule:
> when agent B takes over from agent A, B pays A from its wallet
> if B's move sets things up so that agent C is willing to pay a lot - B profits too

agents get rewarded for setting up good next steps

not just for finishing the task themselves

the result on accelerator design:
> the system discovered a useful design pattern on its own
> no template, no instructions - just payment rules and trial and error

the lesson:
> if your pipeline only produces a result at the end of a long chain,
> the bottleneck is usually "who gets credit for what", not the prompts

a market-based training loop can figure out the right agent sequence

that you'd otherwise have to design by hand

Codex did not become interesting only because the model got stronger.
It became interesting because the product layer started feeling calmer.
As of June 6, 2026, the clean update is this:
• Codex is now centered around GPT-5.5
• OpenAI recommends GPT-5.5 for complex Codex work
• Codex has app, CLI, IDE, cloud, Windows, browser, computer-use, plugins, sites, and annotations
• Claude Code has moved past the Opus 4.7 moment and now has Opus 4.8
• Opus 4.8 adds dynamic workflows, effort control, and better behavior on agentic tasks
This should not be read as:
"Codex won and Claude lost."
The better read:
Codex is winning trust in repo-heavy work because the harness is easier to reason about.
Claude Code still has serious power, but the user has to think harder about model choice, effort level, rate limits, tool permissions, and update channels.
That is the real story.
For coding agents, trust is now part of intelligence.
#
The model frame changed
Opus 4.7 was at the center of the argument in May 2026.
It is no longer the current model frame.
Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28, 2026.
That changes the comparison.
Opus 4.8 is not just a benchmark refresh. Anthropic says it improves on Opus 4.7, keeps regular pricing unchanged, adds effort control, launches dynamic workflows for Claude Code, and makes fast mode cheaper than previous models.
That matters because the trust problem was clear:
users felt Claude Code became unpredictable
The current Anthropic answer is:
give users more control over effort, let Claude Code run larger dynamic workflows, and ship a stronger Opus model
That does not erase the trust problem.
It updates it.
The question is no longer whether Opus 4.7 was the villain.
The question is whether Claude Code can make the right usage pattern obvious enough that users do not have to reverse-engineer the product.
#
The current Codex frame
OpenAI's Codex docs now list GPT-5.5 as the recommended starting model for complex coding, computer use, knowledge work, and research workflows.
That is the key update.
Codex is not just a GPT-5.3 Codex story anymore.
The current model stack is:
• \`gpt-5.5\` for complex Codex work
• \`gpt-5.4\` for strong professional work
• \`gpt-5.4-mini\` for faster lower-cost coding tasks
• \`gpt-5.3-codex-spark\` as a near-instant research preview for Pro users
OpenAI also says older \`gpt-5.2\` and \`gpt-5.3-codex\` references are deprecated in Codex sign-in workflows.
That means older comparisons need to be handled carefully.
If a test used an old Codex model, it is not describing the product today.
The current Codex advantage is not just raw model strength.
It is the product shape:
• worktrees
• reviewable diffs
• app, CLI, IDE, and cloud surfaces
• \`AGENTS.md\` project instructions
• in-app browser
• computer use
• plugins and skills
• remote connections
• sites and annotations for workspace output
That is why Codex feels more like an engineering system than a chat assistant.
It gives the model a place to operate.
#
AGENTS.md is the trust layer
The mechanism is harness engineering.

item.content:encoded:
Viv (@Vtrivedy10)

imo there’s a pretty solid default recipe that everyone should use to optimize a system of
Agent = Model + Harness

you should “train” both

1. Build v1 agent using a sensible base harness and some task specific prompting + tools

2. Harness Engineering using eval tasks that roughly match prod

this is often enough - most companies can get acceptable perf doing this. then they collect traces, mine them for patterns, and make slight tweaks from there

3. SFT using data collected from traces) or synthetic data. Often is good candidate for “distillation tasks” to train a cheaper model while maintaining existing performance

4. RL if you have the bandwidth and ability and desire to create environments and designing rewards that represents the tasks you want your agent to be good at. Push past the SFT behavior of “copying” data from existing model to pushing past in some dimension

5. Light harness engineering again to squeeze any more juice (ex: slight prompting) using the trained model that’s better at your task distribution

this loop will largely be productized as a general purpose recipe for building and improving agents

we’re still in the earliest innings of the world’s companies getting comfortable with steps 1-2 of this loop. Harness engineering will probably be the dominant way ppl will optimize agents

but i expect a large number of companies to onboard through this entire loop on some trial project of interest in the next year

most mfs will grind their DMs, send hundreds of messages a week, and post the occasional random thing on their profile because someone told them they "should be posting."
so their content does nothing.
it's a few disconnected posts with no strategy, consistency, or real purpose, sitting on a profile that prospects glance at and forget.
and then they conclude content doesn't work lol.
now, they're half right.
lazy content genuinely does nothing.
but content done properly is one of the most powerful revenue tools you have, and it does 3 things outbound alone can't.
it books calls on its own, pulling in warm inbound from people who found you rather than the other way around.
it makes your outbound convert better, because every prospect you message checks your profile, and strong content is what convinces them you're worth replying to.
it compounds, building an audience and a reputation over time so that your pipeline keeps getting easier instead of resetting to zero every month.
so let me break down how to make content actually print:
##
Why Content And Outbound Work Better Together
before the how, you need to understand why content matters even if outbound is your main engine.
every single prospect you reach out to does one thing before they reply. they click your profile to see who you are.
what they find in that moment decides whether the conversation goes anywhere.
if they land on a profile with nothing on it, no posts, no proof you know your space, just a name and a job title, your message loses credibility instantly. you look like every other random person sliding into their DMs.
if they land on a profile with a steady stream of sharp, relevant content that proves you deeply understand the problem you solve, your message gains credibility. now you're not a stranger pitching them, you're someone who clearly knows their world, reaching out.
so even if you never wanted content to be a lead source on its own, it still raises your reply rate on everything else you do. it's the credibility layer underneath your entire outbound effort.
and that's before content starts booking calls on its own, which it will once it's running properly.
##
The 3 Types Of Content That Actually Book Calls
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKKasPsXYAAP4Zj?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063369932725796864/freddiexpott/article/2063386291606012208/media/2063381664206643200)
here's where most people go wrong. they post randomly, no structure, no plan, just whatever comes to mind that day.
content that prints is built around 3 specific types, each with a job. you want a mix of all 3, because together they move a stranger from never having heard of you to trusting you enough to have a conversation.
1\. Personal Posts
these are about your journey, your story, your unique takes on your industry.
their job is to build connection. people buy from people, and if you only ever post pure information, you become a faceless account nobody feels anything about. personal posts make prospects feel like they know you, which is what makes them comfortable reaching out.
this isn't about overs

item.content:encoded:
Vox (@Voxyz_ai)

tools go stale. here's how they evolve instead.

workflows change. models change. your standards change. rules you write today might be wrong in three weeks. so every tool needs a patch loop.

didn't trigger when it should have → fix the trigger
triggered when it shouldn't → narrow the scope
used outdated info → update the source of truth
same mistake keeps happening → add a failure mode
you keep editing the same thing by hand → turn that edit into a rule
hasn't been used in a while → archive it

the return on tooling comes from compounding. compounding comes from updating.

This blog is probably going to offend some people.
Good.
Because honestly, I am tired of watching the same cycle repeat every year.
Students enter college with big dreams.
Four years later, most of them leave with excuses.
And before someone starts typing "bro you are generalizing," yes, obviously not everyone.
But if you are from an engineering background, especially a tier-3 or tier-69 college, you know exactly what I am talking about.
This is not a motivational blog.
This is not a "follow your passion" blog.
This is just a collection of observations from my own journey, my friends, people I have worked with, and thousands of students I have seen online.
So let's talk.
For better reading experience read it here:
[Dear Indian Students](https://ramx.in/blog/dear-indian-students)
##
The Dead Crowd
Walk into most engineering classrooms.
Half the class is sleeping.
The other half is scrolling Instagram.
Nobody gives a shit about what is being taught.
And to be fair, most professors don't seem very excited either.
Everybody is just trying to get through the day.
But the problem goes deeper than bad professors.
The real issue is that our education system trained us to memorize, not to explore.
School rewarded us for remembering things.
Not questioning things.
Not building things.
Not experimenting.
Just remember the answer.
Write the answer.
Get the marks.
Repeat.
JEE, boards, entrance exams everything optimized us for scores, not curiosity. So when people enter college, they are already mentally exhausted.
They're waiting for instructions.
* Which course should I watch?
* Which language should I learn?
* Which project should I build?
* Which company should I target?
Every decision is outsourced.
If you want my detailed answers to most of these questions, I wrote an entire FAQ Blog:
[The FAQ](https://ramx.in/blog/faq)
Very few people actually sit down and think:
"What do I want to learn?"
I realized this pretty early.
Within the first few months of college, I figured out something that changed everything for me.
This college is probably not going to get me where I want to go.
And after talking to people from other colleges, I realized something even funnier.
Most colleges are playing the same game.
Different building.
Different logo.
Same shit.
The only thing I could control was myself.
So in the middle of my first year, I started grinding.
Not web development. Not AI. Not any of the trendy stuff.
Graphic design and video editing.
My goal was simple.
Earn money.
Because I knew one thing.
If I wanted freedom to experiment, take risks, build weird things, fail, learn and try again, I needed financial independence.
Nobody was going to hand it to me.
That mindset got me my first internship.
Not because I was special. Not because I was smarter.
I simply accepted reality earlier than most people.
If you want the full story, read my blog:
[How to be me?](https://ramx.in/blog/how-to-be-me-learn-build-and-crush-it)
The biggest lesson?
Nobody is coming to save you.
Not your college. Not your professors. Not your friends.
Certainly not some random YouTube playlist.
##
The Crab Mentality Problem
The second

cold email in 2026 is simple asf
the people who say it's dead are sending 50 emails a day from 3 inboxes wondering why nobody replies lol
that's a hobby
real cold email is 500+ inboxes sending 10,000 emails a day with a simple offer that makes it hard to say no.
the math works every single time IF you give it enough volume to work with
##
why volume beats everything:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKGlKpXWcAAkr4A?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2062498852481925120/scaling%5Fshields/article/2063329359910392293/media/2063111706633465856)
the booking rate at scale is roughly 0.1-0.15%.
that means for every 1,000 emails you send, you book 1 to 1.5 calls. the numbers are CONSISTENT across every niche we've tested
accounting firms, ecom agencies, ai agencies, seo companies, landscaping businesses, marketing agencies. the conversion rate stays roughly the same.
so the question becomes dead simple.
how many calls do you want per month?
if you want 10 calls a month, you need to send about 10,000 emails per month.
that's 330 a day which is achievable with 20 inboxes so most people can do this
if you want 30 calls a month, you need about 30,000 emails per month which is 1,000 a day so you need 60-80 inboxes.
still very doable though.
if you want 150 calls a month, you need about 150,000 emails per month.
that's 5,000 a day and you need 300+ inboxes which is where most people tap out because it feels crazy.
but THIS is the level where cold email stops being inconsistent and starts being a machine
if you want 300 calls a month, you need 200,000+ emails per month. 6,500+ a day. 500+ inboxes.
this is where we operate (my agency)
at this volume it's GENUINELY hard to fail because the math won't let you
cold email is not broken lmfaoo. 200 emails a day is broken.
you're literally not giving the system enough data points to produce a result.
it's like throwing a dart once, missing, and concluding that darts don't work
completely illogical
##
the system that makes this possible:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKGlTUnW8AA8BWk?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2062498852481925120/scaling%5Fshields/article/2063329359910392293/media/2063111855682285568)
the infrastructure is straightforward.
240-800 inboxes warmed up on full admin google workspace accounts. 60-80 domains minimum. each inbox sends about 15 emails per day which keeps deliverability solid without burning any individual inbox
the total volume comes from having HUNDREDS of inboxes running simultaneously
i use frostmailer for the inboxes (i built it, so ofc i'm biased, but the inboxes are $1-2 each and they're full admin accounts that don't go down).
instantly for the sending platform. clay for lead enrichment. and a setter in the unified inbox plus warm calling on every positive reply
the warm calling piece doubled our call booking rate overnight.
ANYONE who replies positively or shows interest gets a phone call within minutes.
"hey bro, saw you replied to my email, wanted to chat quickly about what we can do for you."
that human touch on top o
