Bigger context windows and bolt-on memory don't fix long-horizon agents, because the bottleneck was never how much you can store. It's deciding what the model attends to and that's the layer that is worth building as infrastructure. Every team building autonomous agents eventually meets the same wall. A capable model, given tools and a long task, performs beautifully for twenty steps, then drifts, contradicts itself, and falls apart somewhere around step eighty. The reflex is to reach for more: a model with a longer context window, or a memory system that lets the agent store what it learns and recall it later. Both are reasonable. Neither works the way people expect. Understanding the why points directly at the most valuable, least understood layer in the agent stack.
##
The failure is a loop.
The reason agents degrade isn't a shortage of capability. It's a feedback loop, and it has four links.
It starts with a fact that undermines everything built on top of it: a model's ability to use its context is not uniform across that context, and it gets worse as the context fills. Models reliably use information at the start and end of their context and systematically under-attend to the middle, even when they're built for long inputs. Output reliability falls as input grows even on tasks as trivial as repeating back a list of words, with a single distractor measurably hurting performance and several compounding.
The effective context, which is the part a model can actually reason over reliably, is far smaller than the advertised window and it shrinks as you pack more in. So an agent that accumulates history and tool output as it works is steadily lowering the quality of every step it takes. The growing context manufactures per-step errors.
Per-step error would be tolerable if agents took a few steps. They take many, and the failures multiply rather than add. An agent that is 95% reliable on each step becomes closer to coin flips as the steps increase. This is why long-horizon autonomy has lagged so far behind raw capability. The drifts are also self-reinforcing in nature. One tool call that goes off-trajectory makes the next one significantly more likely. Stack that on the first link and the base error rate is itself climbing as the window fills. That's why agents don't degrade gracefully. They hold, then they unpredictably cliff.
A long task therefore has to put state somewhere outside the model, because language models are stateless. Every call begins blank and retains nothing except what you feed back. The answer so far has been to externalize: scratchpads and progress files, checkpoints, vector stores, dedicated memory layers. Some borrow the operating-system metaphor directly, paging information between the context window and larger external stores; memory products extract facts and re-serve them across sessions. This is correct and necessary, and it looks like a clean resolution. The agent forgets nothing important because everything important lives in durable storage.
Except stored memory is inert. The model cannot reason over a database; it can only reason over what is

##
Key Takeaways
* Statelessness is a design flaw, not a trade-off. Most current agents reset every session, but Hermes puts memory and knowledge first.
* Skills turn the agent into compounding infrastructure. Hermes’ learning loop converts one-off successes into reusable, hierarchical skills that automatically discover and compose across tasks.
* Self-improvement is end-to-end persistent. The stack combines skills, episodic memory, dedicated user profiles, and an automated Curator that prunes and archives stale skills.
* Security is enforced at the system level. Default-on secret redaction, credential pools with automatic rotation, profile isolation, and environment scrubbing make Hermes viable for production and multi-tenant use.
* The model layer is verifiably decentralized. Hermes sits atop Psyche, aligning the agent’s security model with a permissionless, trackable training fabric rather than closed proprietary providers.
In February 2026, Nous Research released Hermes Agent under the MIT license. What began as a single curl command and a GitHub repository quickly distinguished itself from the wave of stateless AI assistants entering the market. Within two months, the project accumulated significant community traction, boasting top rankings on OpenRouter’s leaderboards and token volumes exceeding those of the next-ranked applications by a wide margin.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKCpDA7awAAsXEm?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2062833192890220544/DWFVentures/article/2062897248233787776/media/2062834498589605888)
Source: OpenRouter (
<https://openrouter.ai/apps>
)
Hermes’ growth and traction reflect something beyond just hype: a fundamentally different architecture built around persistent learning, local sovereignty, and deep tool integration. It is an open-source agent framework that can be deployed across multiple environments, including terminals, messaging platforms, and IDEs, connects to more than twenty LLM providers, and ships with over forty built-in tools and adapters for various platforms. Its defining claim is that an agent should compound in capability the longer it works with a user, rather than resetting with every session.
This report examines the stateless problem limiting most current AI agents, outlines Hermes’ architecture and learning mechanisms, and compares it against alternatives.
##
The Stateless Problem
Most AI agents share a critical design constraint: statelessness. Context, prompts, results, and feedback are confined to a single session, and when that session ends, everything is lost. This has been a semi-deliberate decision. Memory is genuinely difficult to implement well, with storage making retrieval a more tedious process, on top of significant engineering costs associated with the required curation, compression and retrieval logic. Stateless APIs are also simpler to operate at scale, and for the larger firms, keeping memory on their own infrastructure preserves platform lock-in. Stateless agents simply presented a lower risk, and more attractive optio

There’s a moment that happens in almost every home service business. It usually happens late, after the trucks are back in the yard and the kids are down.
The owner sits at the kitchen table with a laptop and a stack of paper. The software they pay for every month already did part of the job. It booked the calls. It sent the invoice. But it could not do the one thing that actually makes the business theirs. So they do that part by hand. A spreadsheet on the side. A note in their head. A three-ring binder. Again.
I have watched a thousand versions of that table. And I want to tell you why it exists, why it is about to stop existing, and why we started a company to make sure it does.
##
A promise that got broken
Software was supposed to serve the people doing the work.
That was the whole idea. The tool was meant to disappear into the background so the plumber could plumb, the roofer could roof, the tech could get to the next stop on time. Somewhere along the way, it flipped. The work started bending around the software instead of the software bending around the work.
You know exactly how this feels, because you live it.
Your vendor pushes an interface update on a Friday afternoon, and your crew shows up Monday to a screen that rearranged itself over the weekend, relearning a tool they already knew. You try to turn last month’s job for a good customer into a recurring one, and the software makes you build a brand new job from scratch, as if you had never met them. You want to edit a workflow, rename a feature, add a decline button to your invoice. You are not allowed to touch any of it.
And those are just the daily aggravations. The deeper ones are the parts only someone in your trade would even think to ask for. You want to track refrigerant recovery by job, because EPA Section 608 logs in a binder are not a system, they are a liability waiting for an audit. Your software does not do that. You want your estimator to price by roof pitch, because a 12/12 burns far more labor than a 4/12, between the added surface area and roping off for safety, and your proposal has no idea. It does not do that either. And if you clear land with a herd of goats, you want your map to show which paddock they have already grazed and where the herd is standing right now, because a GPS collar is useless if nothing is reading it. Good luck getting your software to do that.
You called your vendor. You asked for the feature. And you heard the two sentences every operator in this industry has heard at least once: put in a support ticket, and that’s too niche for us to build.
Here is the truth nobody said out loud… it was never too niche. It was just too small for them. The companies serving the trades were built to sell the same product to as many people as possible, which means they build for the middle of the market and never for the edges. The problem is that your business does not live in the middle. Your business lives at the edges. The edges are the reason you win the job, keep the customer, and make the margin. The edges are where the craft is.
Up until now, you either accepted software that almost fit, or you ran the business on paper and

##
i’ve been using Hermes mostly through Telegram for almost 4 months.
which is sick - because i can talk to my agent from anywhere; phone laptop walking around whatever // wherever.
but after using the new Hermes Desktop app, the thing that clicked for me is pretty simple:
> chat (TG, WhatsApp, Discord, etc...) is a great way to talk to your agent. desktop is where you actually see the system around it.
that’s the part i think people are going to underrate.
##
Hermes Desktop gives your agent a home base.
you can see tools.you can see skills.you can see crons.you can see sessions.you can switch profiles.you can see live agent runs.you can see memory/context settings.you can connect local or remote gateways.
if you’ve been operating through Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, texts, or any other chat surface, this is a massive upgrade.
the main character here is visibility.
#
the killer feature: session continuity
the first thing that felt kind of magical:
i could start with my Hermes agent from my phone, then open Hermes Desktop and pick up the same session there.
same agent.same sessions.same skills.same memory.same config.
the conversation doesn’t disappear into a messaging app scrollback.
you can start something on Telegram, then move into Desktop when you need more control, more visibility, or just more screen space.
you can also go the other way: start something in Desktop, leave halfway through, then pick up that same session on your phone in Telegram.
that matters a lot if you actually use agents for work.
because a real agent session is rarely just “send one message, get one answer.”
it turns into:
* checking what happened
* continuing old context
* seeing what tools fired
* finding artifacts
* managing settings
* switching models
* watching context usage
* dealing with approvals
* jumping between different agents/profiles
that stuff is painful when everything is hidden behind chat.
Desktop makes it visible.

item.content:encoded:
North@CreaoAI (@anorth_chen)

Peter这篇文章讲清楚了cloud agent和desktop agent的根本分界：一旦agent离开用户电脑，问题从framework变成了infra contract。

桌面agent默认了很多隐含前提：本地文件系统可信、env里的key可信、用户在线、失败可以手动重试、环境坏了可以重装。

但对cloud agent来说，它要在无人监督、共享硬件、可能被prompt injection影响的代码环境里运行，还要支持被cron、API、以及其他agent调用。

因此在技术范式上，agent runtime未来会越来越像一个小型OS。

很多用户和朋友问过我们对secrets的安全管理问题，这篇文章很好的回答了我们的方案：
我们不去解决sandbox的安全性，这会让我们陷入跟黑客之间的攻防中把业务拖死。换另一个思路：假设sandbox已经被攻破，长期有效的secrets永远不进入sandbox执行边界。让黑客的攻入sandbox后的收益难以覆盖他们的时间和精力成本，他们自然会放弃这件事。

Peter的这篇技术分享文章很好的诠释了我之前说的agent产品难以落地的问题：demo阶段你只需要处理好context管理和tool数量；production阶段真正决定产品可靠性的是这些很无聊的东西：snapshot、JWT、IP allowlist、billing/logging/observability的一致执行管线。

agent is a function with a natural language interface。

agent的业务能力取决于用户的know-how，我们作为平台，帮助用户解决trigger surface、runtime和security boundary等等基建的问题。

item.content:encoded:
Papo Econômico (@opapoeconomico)

A Stripe publicou o mapa global de fraude em pagamentos digitais.

Índia lidera: 30+ bps. A cada 10.000 transações, mais de 30 são golpe.

Brasil logo atrás: 25-30 bps. Um dos piores do planeta.

EUA e Canadá? 5-10 bps. Cinco vezes menos fraude que aqui.

Europa varia muito — França e Bélgica surpreendentemente altos pra países ricos.

O dado mais brutal: África inteira em cinza. Sem dados. 1,4 bilhão de pessoas invisíveis no mapa de pagamentos digitais.

Brasil e Índia têm algo em comum: democratizaram pagamentos digitais rápido. Pix trouxe dezenas de milhões de pessoas pro sistema em 3 anos. UPI na Índia processa 14 bilhões de transações por mês.

Cada nova conta é superfície de ataque. Inclusão financeira sem segurança proporcional é convite aberto.

A Stripe Radar usa ML pra detectar e bloquear fraude em tempo real. Mesmo assim, emergentes dominam o ranking.

O custo de fraude já tá precificado no modelo das fintechs brasileiras — ou vai explodir?

item.content:encoded:
Patrick Collison (@patrickc)

Tyler and I just published a list of the recipients of the New Aesthetics grants: https://newaesthetics.art/grants.

Thank you very much to all who applied. There were far more applications than we expected. We funded 28 grantees and are excited to see what they create.

My reflections on the whole thing:

• Though there are clearly selection dynamics afoot, figuring out some route beyond the current aesthetic moment seems to be of wider interest in the art community than I would have guessed. Many applicants described their dissatisfaction with the status quo, some in strong terms. We had to close applications after a few weeks because there were so many.
• It's too early to call it, but it seems that both beauty as an unapologetic goal (contra much that is in modernist and contemporary approaches), and ways to channel pre-modern styles into something new for the present era, are of growing interest.
• The awards made me reflect on the perhaps obvious issue of how hard it must be for an artist to persistently do something new: schools, galleries, buyers, etc., all have structurally embedded preferences as well. These individual awards made me wonder what form supporting new clusters could take.
• Architecture seems to me like the discipline most ripe for new ideas. One correspondent observed: "American architects are somewhat constrained by the association with the academy, in addition to the well known regulation issues. There is a tendency to overthink things so that the designs are formally interesting to someone deep in the conversation, but lacking poetry and magic. There are more firms in Europe, South America and beyond that “just do things” (especially in places where it is easier to build)." This was evident in the submissions.
• AI seems to be making people rethink things in a quite fundamental way, just as urbanization/industrialization/popularization of photography did at the end of the 19th century. For some that will mean interesting new forms of AI-augmented art, but the effects of the rethinking will likely be wider.
• Arts funding is clearly as precarious and scarce as ever. That's unfortunate, but it probably also means that individual actors can have meaningful impact, and I encourage others to get involved if interested.
• There's a lot to know that is not written down, and I'm very grateful to those who have helped and advised me along the way.

🔗 A Call for New Aesthetics

# New Aesthetics Grants
* [Andy Allen](https://notbor.ing/)
Andy is highlighting the aesthetics and cultural impact of software.
* Luke Burgis
* [Spencer Chang](https://spencer.place)
Spencer Chang is an artist and engineer making software you can touch and will create a participatory artwork that preserves and activates our traces across the Internet.
* [Adam Davies and Jack Marsh](https://www.notquitepast.com/about/)
Adam Davies and Jack Marsh (Not Quite Past) work on what they call the future's recovery of the past, starting with AI-designed Delft tiles.
* [Alihan Dumankaya](https://estudio.ad/)
Alihan Dumankaya is an architect based in Barcelona who explores architectural languages and ways of creating places with more life.
* [Megan Gafford](https://www.fashionablylatetakes.com/p/towards-a-new-aesthetic)
I’m going to try to invent a new ornamental style of architecture through drawing, because just as writing is thinking, drawing is imagining.
* [Mark Gorenstein](https://oeuvre.art/)
œuvre editions aims to marry the traditional crafts of printing and bookmaking with modern technological and aesthetic developments.
* [Ruben Hanssen](https://theaestheticcity.com/towards-a-new-aesthetics/)
A short documentary series on the YouTube channel The Aesthetic City, exploring the future of aesthetics, connecting time-tested principles with the latest technologies.
* [Matthew Henderson](https://x.com/instance%5F11)
My work explores how designing solely with code can take full advantage of digital fabrication and thereby enable a world where all precious things are unique.
* [Chelsea Hodson](https://www.rosebooks.co/)
Rose Books is an independent publisher in Sedona, Arizona, which will use the New Aesthetics grant to support the production and operations costs for publication of the next two titles.
* Rui Huang
* [Zahra Jewanjee](https://www.zjewanjee.com)
Zahra Jewanjee's multidisciplinary practice oscillates between painting, photography, sculpture, and found materials, echoing interconnectedness and interdependence within nature.
* [Joseph Jutras](https://www.institute-of-traditional-architecture.org/)
Jutras is an advocate for beauty in our built environment and will use the grant towards founding a full-time classical architecture academy.
* [Ben Lee](https://www.linkedin.com/in/benlee01)
My work leverages emerging 21st-century tools to move beyond default building practices, aiming to cultivate a vibrant architectural language that defines the visual character and aesthetic ambition of our generation.
* [Bhumika Mukherjee](https://bhumikamukherjee.com/)
My work tries to depict the projected abstraction of life as perceived by life.
* [Karyn Nakamura](https://karynnakamura.com)
Building a studio that translates between technology and culture through creative direction, experimental R&D, and technical production.
* [Not Nothing](https://www.notnothing.ooo/)
Not Nothing publishes unfashionable work from hermits and informants, for human and non-human readers, while experimenting with how books are constructed so their discourse may outlast them.
* [Sam Peitz](https://x.com/samdape)
We use AI in ways that flatten us to a common denominator. Experimenting with ones that do the opposite, stripping design back to its fundamentals.
* [Hamzah Randhawa](https://x.com/haramzah2/status/2058709416547901688?s=20)
Creating a workshop/lab to prototype both temporary and permanent modular 3D-printed and CNC milled bespoke ceiling facades inspired by various cultural heritages.
* [Michiel Rauws](https://michielrauws.me/sf-undergrounding)
Power cables make San Francisco streets look like we live in the year 1900, but not for much longer.
* [San Modern](https://sanmodern.com)
The grant will support our development of a silent, analog meditation timer—a first step toward our mission of bringing more care, wonder and aesthetic conviction back into everyday objects.
* [Kristina Saint](https://www.kvsaint.com/)

item.content:encoded:
Ramya Chinnadurai 🚀 (@code_rams)

A single agent running 50 tasks is one person who quits at task 20 and reports it done.

A dynamic workflow is a team.
One writes the plan. A fleet runs it, one job each. A separate agent tries to break the result.

No agent audits its own work. The goal never drifts.

Turned a 45-minute job into 8 minutes for me this week. Full breakdown in the post.

The 5-Channel Funnel That Added $307K MRR for us in a Single Quarter
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1909705035052990467/pnfX3LA__normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2062512037541130240/itsalexvacca)
[Alex Vacca](http://x.com/i/article/2062512037541130240/itsalexvacca)

[12K](http://x.com/i/article/2062512037541130240/itsalexvacca/status/2062623990192251082/analytics)
Most founders try to fix the wrong end of the funnel.
Reply rates dip, so they rewrite subject lines. Close rates soften, so they rebuild the pitch deck. Months disappear into optimizing the bottom of a system that's actually starving at the top. The constraint was never the copy. The machine just wasn't taking in enough qualified people to begin with.
We spent Q1 proving the opposite case. 100,000 unique visitors to the site. 200+ meetings booked. $307K in new MRR added, on a business already past $7M ARR and built without a dollar of outside money. None of that came from a cleverer email. It came from treating lead generation as the lever everything else hangs off, then building the rest of the funnel so almost nothing we generated leaked back out.
There's a lazy version of this idea going around, the one that says a strong top of funnel earns you the right to a sloppy bottom. That reading is wrong, and acting on it gets expensive fast. Pour 100,000 visitors into a quarter and a 5% leak stops being a rounding error. It's thousands of in-market buyers walking out with your acquisition cost in their pocket. At that scale a weak funnel doesn't just underperform. It bleeds money in direct proportion to how much traffic you feed it.
So we built both ends on purpose. Here's the whole system, stage by stage, with the actual stack behind it.
#
Why volume changes the entire problem
A funnel that handles 2,000 visitors a quarter and one that handles 100,000 are not the same machine at two sizes. They break in different places.
At low volume, your problem is genuine scarcity. You don't have enough at-bats, so every conversation has to convert, and the work lives downstream: sharper targeting, better calls, tighter follow-up. Most GTM advice is written for this world, which is why it fixates on messaging.
At high volume, scarcity becomes a routing problem. The leads already exist. The real question is whether your system can catch, score, and route them before they cool off. The bottleneck shifts from "can we get a meeting" to "can we hold the 94 people who raised a hand but weren't ready to book today." Lose them and you've built an expensive way to hand buyers to your competitors.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-EgbuaUAAr-Sp?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2062512037541130240/itsalexvacca/article/2062623990192251082/media/2062512847092076544)
Leads lost to a 5% capture leak, by quarterly traffic
That chart is the whole reason we refuse to treat the bottom of the funnel as optional. A 5% leak that costs 100 leads at low volume costs 5,000 at ours. Founders between $500K and $5M usually keep optimizing for scarcity long after their real problem quietly became volume management. We built the entire funnel around the volume problem, in four stages.
#
Stage 1: Five channels into one pipe
Traffic comes from five places, and the number isn't the point.e backend. What matters is that the channels are coordinated and they all empty into the sam
Automated outbound, LinkedIn content, LinkedIn Ads, Google Ads, and SEO. A prospect might catch a team member's LinkedIn p

How we made continuous trace intelligence possible at scale

If you run an agent in production, some part of your day is probably going through countless production logs to see if anything looks interesting. You know there’s good intel in there somewhere, but the data doesn’t tell you what question you should be asking, or what SQL query would capture it.
We’ve been thinking about this problem at Braintrust for a long time, and Topics is the solution that lets you analyze traces with intelligence at scale. Like Brainstore, it’s one of the small number of big, concentrated technical bets we’ve made on owning a primitive end-to-end rather than stitching together off-the-shelf pieces. With Brainstore, the bet was on the storage and query layer. With Topics, the bet is on the intelligence layer that sits on top.
In order to find patterns you didn’t know to look for, you need to run this intelligence layer over every trace. We call this active observability. The problem is that LLM traces aren’t shaped like anything the standard tools expect. The standard NLP toolkit assumes documents that are roughly uniform in shape and size. Topic modeling wants bag-of-words documents in the hundreds of tokens. Sentiment analysis wants a sentence or paragraph. Off-the-shelf clustering on embeddings wants inputs that fit inside an embedding model’s context window.
Agent traces don’t look like that. A single production trace can be millions of tokens of conversation history, tool calls, intermediate reasoning, retrieved context, and serialized application state. They arrive at high volume, they keep updating after they’re “done,” and the interesting behavior is usually buried in a few spans out of hundreds. If you embed the raw trace, you get noisy clusters dominated by surface features like message length or tool name frequency. If you summarize first with an LLM, you blow your budget. If you sample aggressively, you miss the long tail, which is where the bugs usually live.
The insight that drove Topics is inspired by Anthropic’s Clio paper. Instead of trying to embed or classify the raw trace, you ask an LLM to do one job: summarize the trace along a single dimension in a sentence or two. Then you embed that summary, cluster the embeddings, and name the clusters with a second LLM pass. The trace itself never has to fit in an embedding model’s context window, and the downstream pipeline never has to know anything about agents, tools, or token counts.
This sounds like a small move, and architecturally it is. Operationally it changes everything. Once the LLM summary step exists, the same downstream pipeline works for any dimension you care about: task, issues, sentiment, and custom categories you define for your product all flow through the same embed, cluster, name, and classify stages.
Three design goals fall out of that bet. First, the LLM summary step has to be tightly scoped, batch-friendly, and cost-efficient enough to run on every trace.
